stories.headline: 45 days in hell: Ukraine’s underground war with Putin
stories.claim: Ukrainian troops describe fighting a covert underground war in Kupyansk's gas pipelines during Operation Veles.
stories.summary: Ukrainian soldiers have described an underground counter-offensive in decommissioned gas pipelines near Kupyansk in the Kharkiv region, known as Operation Veles. According to the accounts gathered by The Telegraph, the operation killed around 100 Russian soldiers and captured 30, while Ukrainian forces reclaimed just over nine miles of territory. Troops spent weeks in cramped, toxic tunnels, some for up to 45 days, facing gas, dust, infections and close-quarters firefights separated by sandbag barricades. Drones and unmanned ground vehicles were used alongside above-ground assault teams that cut Russian supply lines. The report shows how drones and subterranean fighting are reshaping the front line.

stories.headline: Brazil inflation remains above goal despite softer-than-expected October reading
stories.claim: Brazil's 12-month inflation rose to 4.63% in October, below forecasts but still above the central bank's target range.
stories.summary: Brazil's annual inflation edged up to 4.63% in October from 4.58% in September, coming in below the 4.73% that economists had expected in a Reuters poll. Monthly prices rose 0.14%, slower than the 0.25% forecast, as food and drink costs climbed while transport and housing eased. Inflation remains well above the central bank's 3% target, with a tolerance of 1.5 points either side. The central bank paused its easing cycle last week and held the Selic rate at 13.75%, and policymakers have vowed to keep rates high. Analysts say rate cuts are unlikely before March, and the weaker real and higher long-term yields after President Lula's re-election reflect fiscal worries.

Food and beverage prices rose 1.04% on the month, while transport fell 0.59% and housing fell 0.51%.

Capital Economics expects easing to resume only once inflation trends down, probably from March, and fiscal reform is needed to cut risk premia.
President Lula's re-election last month weakened the real and pushed long-term rates and inflation forecasts higher.
stories.market_take: Inflation below forecast gives some relief, but the central bank's hold and fiscal worries keep the real and Brazilian rates under pressure.

stories.headline: Germany Plans to Ready Coal and Oil Power Plants to Save Gas
stories.claim: German parliament passes emergency law to reactivate mothballed coal plants and gas-fired capacity plans to protect winter gas supplies.
stories.summary: Germany's parliament has given final approval to emergency legislation that lets the government bring mothballed coal-fired power plants back online, a move aimed at saving gas before winter. The upper house signed off on the measure alongside a package to speed up renewable energy, including a rule that classifies renewables as a matter of public security and sets minimum land each federal state must allow for wind farms. Economy minister Robert Habeck called the step painful but necessary. Gas storage was only about a third full when the war in Ukraine broke out and had reached roughly 63% by Friday, well short of the 90% goal, so industry lobby the BDI has urged saving every cubic metre. Environmental groups say it risks Germany missing basic climate targets, since Germany had planned to phase out coal by 2030. Separately, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has scaled back planned new gas plants to 10 gigawatts by 2032, from 20 gigawatts, with tenders to be hydrogen-ready and European Commission approval expected soon.
key_points: Germany's parliament has passed emergency legislation to reactivate mothballed coal-fired power plants to support electricity supply.
The package also classifies renewable energy expansion as a matter of public security and sets minimum wind farm land per federal state.
Gas storage reached about 63% capacity, short of a 90% target, with experts saying the goal is needed to get through winter.
The BDI industry body warned of a grave gas shortage and sharp drop in industrial output without further savings.
Chancellor Merz plans gas plant auctions next year totalling 10 GW by 2032, down from an earlier 20 GW target, which must still win European Commission approval.

stories.headline: Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update
stories.claim: Microsoft confirms October Windows update causes SQL Server linked server connections to stay open and degrade performance.
stories.summary: Microsoft has acknowledged that a change in the October 13 update (KB5126646) stops SQL Server from closing connections created by linked server queries. Connections to external databases such as PostgreSQL and Oracle can pile up over time and slow server performance. Administrators can manually close idle connections or restart the SQL service, though both can interrupt active work. A mitigation is available only through Microsoft business support, with an out-of-band update expected within days. The bug reportedly affects all Windows versions except Windows 11 26H2, including Windows Server back to 2012. It follows an earlier October 2026 Windows Server update that caused Exchange Server problems.

stories.summary: Nvidia's market value fell below $4 trillion on Thursday, with shares down as much as 14% in early trading, after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned. Huang admitted on Sunday to a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China, and the New York Times later reported a relationship with Nvidia vice-president Kimberly Powell. Its third-quarter results are due on Tuesday, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded the stock this week, with credit default swap costs near a record.

stories.headline: Google Deepmind shifts genomics AI from bulk tissue predictions to single cell type resolution with AlphaGenome 2
stories.claim: Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, which predicts how DNA variants affect specific human cell types.
stories.summary: Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, a genomics AI model that predicts how genetic variants affect specific human cell types rather than averaged bulk tissue. It was trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from 68 human and mouse tissues. On a benchmark of 28 immune cell types, it identified about 30% of causal variants, compared with 16% for its predecessor's fine-tuned version, and correctly predicted the direction of gene change in 43% of cases against 23%. The model is available now for noncommercial research via API, and is not approved for clinical diagnostics. DeepMind plans to combine it with Gemini 4 on its Google Antigravity platform.
key_points: AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional model that takes a specific cell state as input, unlike its bulk-tissue predecessor.
It was trained on over 107 million cell profiles from 68 human and mouse tissues.
On the TenK10K benchmark it found about 30% of causal variants, against 16% for the earlier fine-tuned model.
It can predict DNA methylation and chart chromatin accessibility, and can adapt to new experiments without retraining.

DeepMind plans to add AlphaGenome 2 features to Google Antigravity alongside Gemini 4.

stories.headline: First FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation in PSMA PET imaging granted to Cu-64 SAR-bisPSMA in biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer – Company Announcement - FT.com
stories.claim: Clarity Pharmaceuticals wins FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for its Cu-64 SAR-bisPSMA prostate cancer imaging agent.
stories.summary: Sydney-listed Clarity Pharmaceuticals has received FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for its copper-64 SAR-bisPSMA imaging agent, the first such designation in the history of PSMA PET imaging. The agent is designed to detect prostate cancer recurrence after a rise in PSA levels, where existing agents miss disease in many patients. Company data showed a 78% detection rate in a Phase II trial, more than double the 36% for gallium-68 PSMA-11 in the same patient group. Two pivotal Phase III trials, AMPLIFY and CLARIFY, have finished recruiting, with topline data expected in the first half of 2027. The designation could speed review, but approval still depends on those trial results.

stories.headline: AI Traffic Outpaces Email, Social and Paid Search in Retail Value: Adobe

The club confirmed the departure in a statement, with eight points from 10 games and only one league win. Carrick had been interim boss from January 2026 and had led the side to a third-place finish and Champions League qualification. Reports point to a dressing-room rift, and the club is expected to appoint Mauricio Pochettino, who reportedly agreed a verbal deal and whose release from US Soccer could cost around $10m. Minority owners Ineos are looking for a fourth permanent manager in three years.
key_points: Manchester United confirmed Michael Carrick has left his role as men's first-team head coach.
United sit 18th in the 20-team Premier League with eight points from 10 games, the worst league start in their history.
Carrick had guided the side to third place and Champions League qualification after taking over in January 2026.
Reports point to a dressing-room rift; the club will appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.
Mauricio Pochettino is reported to be the overwhelming favourite, with compensation of about $10m (£7.4m) being discussed with US Soccer.
Next match is away to Liverpool in the Premier League, roughly two weeks after the international break.

stories.claim: Zelenskyy urges Europe to become a regular part of Ukraine peace talks as EU leaders debate who should represent them.
stories.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy pressed EU governments to become a regular part of Ukraine peace negotiations, speaking at a European Political Community summit in Dublin. Two days of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday without a breakthrough and without European officials present. Witkoff and Kushner were to meet Putin in Moscow and then brief Zelenskyy in Dublin. EU leaders remain split on who should represent the bloc: Kaja Kallas and Costa are favoured by some, while Macron insists Europe must first agree its own position. The issue will return at Friday's informal European Council.

stories.headline: Putin suggests no Ukraine compromise in meeting with US envoys
stories.claim: Putin signals no compromise on Ukraine demands during televised Kremlin talks with US envoys, but offers a short local truce in Kostyantynivka.
stories.summary: Vladimir Putin signalled on Thursday that Russia will not soften its hardline terms for ending the war in Ukraine, even as he offered a short-term ceasefire in the frontline city of Kostyantynivka. Meeting Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the Kremlin after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, he ruled out foreign peacekeepers, calling them a 'continuation of war', and insisted on control of the four regions Moscow has annexed. The Kremlin televised the opening exchange, which was unusual. The envoys then flew to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a European summit, where Zelenskyy also said new limits on the Starshield satellite internet service were hurting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-drones. Putin's remarks dampened hopes of a near-term deal, and European leaders are pressing for a seat at the table.

stories.summary: Meta has disabled Russell Brand's social media accounts on its platforms, including Instagram and Facebook, after he was sentenced earlier this week. stories.headline: Two Indian police officers killed in Kashmir shooting
stories.claim: Two policemen found shot dead in Indian-administered Kashmir, a day after gunmen wounded three paramilitary troops in Kulgam.
stories.summary: Two Indian policemen were found shot dead in Kishtwar, about 220km south-east of Srinagar, in Indian-administered Kashmir on 12 November, a day after they were reported missing. The killings came one day after suspected rebels on motorbikes opened fire on Central Reserve Police Force members at a checkpoint in Kulgam district, wounding three. The attacks follow Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent claim of a year without CRPF casualties, the first in 47 years. Police have not released details and have not assigned blame, though a local legislator blamed 'terrorists' and vowed revenge. India regularly accuses Pakistan of arming rebels, a charge Islamabad denies. The back-to-back attacks raise fresh security concerns in the disputed Himalayan region.

stories.headline: Kayla Smith admits murdering love rival Chloe Watson in Leeds

stories.summary: At Leeds Crown Court, 18-year-old Kayla Smith has admitted murdering 16-year-old Chloe Watson Dransfield, whom she stabbed to death in a pre-planned fight over a boy. Smith had first pleaded guilty to manslaughter, then changed her plea to murder on the second day of her trial. The court heard that Chloe went to Smith's home in Leeds with her boyfriend Blake Dowling, who had been in a relationship with both girls, and that Smith had threatened to stab her. Chloe was stabbed five times in the neck and back and bled to death in March. Dowling and Archie Rycroft, 20, both deny murder and manslaughter charges, and their trial continues. Mr Justice Cavanagh KC will sentence Smith after the trial, and the only sentence for murder is life imprisonment with a minimum term to be set.

stories.headline: Two Iranian men found guilty in UK of assisting Iranian intelligence

stories.summary: Two Iranian men have been convicted at Woolwich Crown Court of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iranian intelligence. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was found guilty of two offences and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, of one offence under the National Security Act. stories.headline: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators in Mississippi
stories.claim: Democrat Scott Colom won a close Mississippi Senate race, becoming the state's first Black US senator in over 150 years.
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has won a close race in Mississippi to become the state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction, and only the third Black senator in US history. The result is historic in a deeply conservative southern state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1982 and had not seated a Black senator since 1875. Colom follows Hiram Revels, seated 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, who served 1875 to 1881 and was the first Black person to serve a full Senate term. Colom credited mobilising young voters and the state's large Black population, with students at Jackson State University among those backing him. The win comes amid Republicans' broader midterm losses, which the BBC report suggests were shaped by the same forces. Colom's victory is a notable shift in Mississippi politics.

stories.headline: Crowds fill Lima streets for Pope Leo's emotional return to Peru
stories.claim: Pope Leo draws huge crowds in Lima on the second day of an emotional visit to his adopted homeland, Peru.
stories.summary: Pope Leo, the first Peruvian to lead the Catholic Church, drew crowds that flooded central Lima on Thursday as he began the second day of an emotional homecoming. A record crowd of around 3 million reportedly lined the city's streets on Wednesday, when he told a cheering audience that he considered Peru his homeland. Originally from Chicago, Leo spent about 20 years as a missionary and bishop in Peru and holds both US and Peruvian citizenship. He is on the final leg of a three-country South American tour, only weeks after lung cancer surgery, and urged President Keiko Fujimori to heal the country's divisions after a narrow election win marred by fraud claims. Peru's crime problem and the clergy abuse scandal also featured in his remarks.

stories.headline: Clean-up begins as oil spill shuts 18 Kent beaches

stories.summary: Eighteen beaches on the Isle of Thanet in Kent, including Margate, Broadstairs and Ramsgate, have been closed after significant deposits of oil washed ashore. Thanet District Council reported the incident on Wednesday evening, and the Environment Agency is investigating with the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which has aircraft searching the area. Swimming has been advised against and dog walkers urged to keep away. A bathing ban was also imposed in Cliftonville in May after smaller oil deposits were found.

stories.summary: A 42-year-old GP from Shropshire, Annette Quilter, has become the first patient in the UK to receive an NHS dose of teplizumab, a drug that can delay the onset of insulin-dependent Type 1 diabetes. The infusion was given at Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham this week. Quilter was diagnosed with Stage 2 Type 1 diabetes in the summer and was found eligible after screening. The treatment involves one 30-minute infusion a day for 14 days, and it has been available on the NHS since June 2026 for eligible children over eight and adults with Stage 2 disease.

stories.headline: ‘Blind spot’ no longer: Austria targets Russian espionage with new law
stories.claim: Austria's government approved draft law tightening espionage rules, with up to five-year sentences for spying on international bodies.
stories.summary: Austria's government has approved draft legislation to tighten its espionage laws, closing a loophole that left spying on other countries and international organisations less clearly covered. The bill proposes up to five years in prison for espionage against EU institutions and bodies such as the UN, OSCE and IAEA based in Austria, and raises the maximum sentence for spying on Austria itself from five to 10 years. It would also criminalise recruiting so-called disposable agents for foreign intelligence. Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger framed the move as ending Vienna's reputation as a spy hub, and it forms part of a wider shift in policy toward Russia. Austria has expelled eight Russian diplomats since March 2025 and has had at least three satellite installations removed from Russian diplomatic sites. The bill is expected to pass parliament next year and take effect in February 2027.

stories.headline: ‘A second chance’: children guilty of serious offences will no longer have to declare criminal records
stories.claim: UK government proposes lifting lifelong criminal record disclosure for many offences committed as a child in England and Wales.
stories.summary: Children convicted of robbery, supplying drugs to other children, violent disorder and affray would no longer have to disclose those offences for life under new government proposals in England and Wales. Instead, disclosure periods would be shortened: five and a half years for non-custodial sentences and 11 years for sentences of up to two years, while longer custodial sentences would still carry lifelong disclosure. Fines for childhood offences would no longer need to be disclosed, against six months under current law. Justice minister Jake Richards framed the plans as second chances that could boost youth employment and reduce the number of children in custody. The proposals are subject to consultation, and campaigners such as the charity Unlock have welcomed them, while employers say criminal records are the second biggest barrier to hiring disadvantaged people.

stories.headline: ‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?

Driver Wang Bing, who runs a route between Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan island, says his fuel cost is about 1.1 yuan (12p) per kilometre against more than 2 yuan for diesel. It has also teamed up with Octopus Energy to open its first European 'mega hubs' in the UK in 2027, with more than 30 across Europe by 2035. Only about a third of China's zero-emission trucks used swapping in 2024, and the model locks drivers to specific providers.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affair scandal; Colette Kress named interim chief
stories.claim: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO and board member with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and Harvey Jones is first independent chair.
stories.summary: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that turned the chipmaker into a company worth roughly $4 trillion. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor, and longtime director Harvey Jones becomes the company's first independent chair. The exit follows Huang's admission of an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed whom US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security, as well as a second relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reports to him. Nvidia's shares opened down about 10% and had already lost roughly $600 billion in value since the investigation was announced on 8 November. The board's statement did not mention the allegations, and the company's first quarterly results without Huang are due on November 17. Huang holds about 3.6% of the company, and prediction markets reportedly favour Ian Buck as a successor.

stories.headline: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
stories.claim: Microsoft says Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are now permanently vulnerable, with no further security updates after October 2026.
stories.summary: Microsoft has told customers still running Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to treat those versions as 'permanently vulnerable', as the final security updates for them were released on 13 October. Support for those versions ended in October 2025, and an extended security update programme ran until April 2026 before a further six-month extension. The November update fixes nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server Subscription Edition, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft is no longer testing the older versions for vulnerabilities, leaving organisations that have not migrated exposed.
key_points: Microsoft released the final Exchange 2016 and 2019 security updates on 13 October 2026.
Microsoft now says those versions should be considered permanently vulnerable and urges immediate upgrades.
The November update patches nine flaws in Exchange Server SE, including critical remote code execution flaw CVE-2026-118207.
Extended security support had been promised to end in April 2026 but was extended by six months.
Organisations still on the old versions face unpatched risk and must migrate to Subscription Edition or Exchange Online.

stories.headline: Synchron Pauses Trials of Its Brain Implant Due to Performance Issues
stories.claim: Synchron pauses enrollment in trials of its second-generation brain implant after a lead performance issue; restructuring under way.
stories.summary: Brain-computer interface startup Synchron has paused enrolment in clinical trials of its second-generation Stentrode after the device underperformed in early participants, WIRED reports. The company says the problem lies with the lead, the cable carrying signals to the implanted electronics, and that no safety issues have been identified. Synchron is upgrading the whole system and bringing lead design and manufacturing in-house before resuming enrolment. It is also restructuring, cutting jobs and scaling back in New York while hiring about a dozen engineers in San Diego. The setback matters because the trials are needed before the US Food and Drug Administration can consider marketing approval.
key_points: Enrolment in the second-generation Stentrode trial has been paused after a performance issue with the lead cable.
Synchron says the pause was its own decision, not FDA-directed, and no device safety issues have been found.
The company is redesigning the whole system and bringing lead manufacturing in-house, with enrolment to resume after upgrades.
Restructuring involves job cuts and a smaller New York footprint, with about a dozen openings in San Diego.
Synchron was valued at nearly $1 billion after a $200 million round last year, and rival Neuralink was reportedly valued up to $42 billion.

stories.headline: Mac malware doesn't need a security flaw when users do the work
stories.claim: Bitdefender report finds adware rising sharply as attackers use browser scams to trick Mac users into bypassing Apple's protections.
stories.summary: Mac malware is increasingly spreading without exploiting any software flaw, because attackers are tricking users into disabling Apple's protections themselves. Bitdefender's September 2026 macOS Threat Landscape Report analysed more than 1.5 billion security events collected between August 2025 and July 2026. Adware's share of detections, excluding web and document threats, jumped from 22.6% in the previous report to 34.4%. Trojans remain the largest category but fell from 51.8% to 45.2%, while potentially unwanted apps dropped from 25.3% to 20.4%. The shift matters for Mac owners, since social-engineering attacks bypass the security Apple builds into macOS and are harder to patch.
key_points: Bitdefender's September 2026 macOS report covers more than 1.5 billion security events from August 2025 to July 2026.
Adware rose from 22.6% to 34.4% of detections, excluding web and document threats.
Trojans are still the largest category, but their share fell from 51.8% to 45.2%.
Potentially unwanted apps fell from 25.3% to 20.4%.
Attackers increasingly rely on browser scams that persuade users to bypass Apple's security checks.

stories.headline: Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor
stories.claim: IBM unveils Nighthawk r3 quantum processor with 520 qubits, due in 2027, as a step to a 2029 fault-tolerant system.
stories.summary: IBM has unveiled Nighthawk r3, a next-generation quantum processor with 520 qubits, more than four times the 120 qubits of the Nighthawk r2 released in September. IBM says it will run 10,000 quantum operations, up from 7,500, while keeping the same speed and accuracy. Due in 2027, two Nighthawk r3 chips will be linked via 10 chip-to-chip couplers into a single system of 1,040 qubits. The work is a step towards Starling, IBM's planned fault-tolerant machine targeted for 2029, which aims to run circuits of 100 million operations on 200 logical qubits. IBM is also pairing its quantum chips with classical supercomputers, including a recent Oak Ridge National Laboratory setup.
key_points: Nighthawk r3 will have 520 qubits, over four times the 120 in Nighthawk r2.

IBM is combining quantum systems with high-performance classical computers, including at Oak Ridge and RIKEN in Japan.
stories.market_take: Limited near-term effect on share prices, though IBM benefits from positioning in quantum computing.

stories.headline: Maga architects blame Big Tech and AI data centres for midterms rout
stories.claim: Republicans blame Big Tech and AI data centres for midterm losses, as markets fall over fears of tougher AI regulation.
stories.summary: Republicans are blaming Big Tech and AI data centres for their midterm losses, and investors reacted sharply on Thursday. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% and more than $2 trillion of market value was wiped out, reversing Wednesday's gains, as fears grew that an incoming Democratic Congress would crack down on AI. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom won a Senate seat against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by 4,669 votes, after campaigning for a pause on new data centres. Ohio's Democrat Sherrod Brown also won on a platform against data-centre expansion, and 40 of 41 local ballot measures on data centres went against the industry. Tesla and SpaceX, both controlled by Elon Musk, fell sharply. Democrats now hold 55 Senate seats, according to the reported count.
key_points: The Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday, wiping out over $2 trillion in market value.
Investors fear an incoming Democratic Congress could regulate AI and restrict data-centre buildout.
Scott Colom won the Mississippi Senate race by 4,669 votes out of 962,237 counted.
An NBC exit poll found a majority of voters called AI data centres a crucial or major factor.
Tesla and SpaceX, controlled by Elon Musk, were among the sharpest decliners.
stories.market_take: Investors are pricing in tougher AI regulation and data-centre curbs, hitting AI-linked tech stocks.

stories.headline: ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live uses conversational context to stop voice agents from cutting off callers mid-sentence

stories.summary: ElevenLabs has released two speech-to-text models, Scribe v3 for recorded audio and Scribe v3 Live for real-time use. stories.headline: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
stories.claim: Hackers used a flawed ScreenConnect plugin, RMM+, to infect at least 288 machines across 48 organisations.
stories.summary: Hackers have used a third-party ScreenConnect extension to install malware on at least 288 machines across 48 organisations, most of them managed IT service providers. Security firm Huntress first flagged the campaign, which hit all the endpoints within 90 minutes. The malware kit, SCKit, installs a hidden remote-access client and tries to spread to technicians and their customers. Huntress traced the entry point to a possible authentication weakness in the RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, where a blank access key is accepted. ConnectWise has disabled five extensions in about 400 environments, though it has not confirmed how the attackers got in. Administrators are warned that disabling extensions alone will not remove the malware.
key_points: At least 288 machines across 48 organisations have been infected via a ScreenConnect extension.
The malware toolkit, SCKit, installs a hidden ScreenConnect client to keep access.
The flaw is linked to RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accept a blank access key.
ConnectWise has disabled five extensions in about 400 environments where they were installed.
Administrators should avoid investigating through ScreenConnect and remove malware before reconnecting machines.
stories.market_take: No clear listed-company impact; ConnectWise is privately owned.

stories.headline: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
stories.claim: Artists and game developers are using satirical video games to mock Trump White House propaganda games and the Iran war.
stories.summary: Video game creators and artists are pushing back against the Trump administration's use of games as political propaganda. The White House launched an official browser game arcade in September, with titles based on Flappy Bird, Snake and Tetris, which pushed immigration and other policies; it was removed days after The Tetris Company threatened copyright action. Now the anonymous collective The Secret Handshake has released free satirical games, Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell and Nuuk 'Em All, which have been played more than 350,000 times online. Another developer has made Tax Evaders, a Space Invaders-style game built on the open-source Godot engine. The piece frames the trend as a counter to the gamification of politics amid rising fuel and grocery prices linked to the Iran war.
key_points: The White House launched an official browser game collection called Arcade in early September, later removed after copyright complaints.
The Tetris Company said it took copyright infringement very seriously after the White House used its game style.

stories.headline: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
stories.claim: Caine Prize clears Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza of using AI to write his prize-winning story.

stories.headline: US workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and winning

An Ernst and Young survey from July to August 2026 found nearly 70% of state and local agencies have adopted or are implementing generative AI. Unions are also pushing back on 'bossware', AI tools that monitor, rank and discipline staff. The company, which has its site in Ivry-sur-Seine near Paris, is betting that power has become the scarcest resource in orbit as satellite constellations and orbital data centres grow. Instead of the specialised III-V cells most rivals use, Gama adapts high-volume terrestrial silicon cells and targets six-month lead times once its line is running. Wing is sold as a complete power system including sun-tracking, power management and optional storage. Gama has a signed partnership with Eclipse Space from September, with a first demonstration unit due in summer 2027. The round will fund the production line, testing and around 60 engineering hires, tripling its 30-person team.

stories.headline: Democrat wins Mississippi Senate race in historic upset
stories.claim: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a historic upset.
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has won the Mississippi Senate race, unseating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that Donald Trump carried by 22 points in 2024. The 43-year-old district attorney becomes the first Black senator from Mississippi in more than 140 years and the first Democrat to win the seat since 1982. The race was decided by less than half a percentage point after a week of counting, with the Associated Press calling it late on Wednesday. Colom campaigned on rising living costs, which he tied to Trump's policies including the war in Iran and higher fuel prices. The result is part of a wider Democratic sweep in the 3 November midterms, in which Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and won control of both chambers of Congress. Only the Alaska race, where Republican Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, remains uncalled.
key_points: Scott Colom, a 43-year-old Democrat and district attorney, beat Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by less than 0.5 per cent with 99 per cent of votes counted.
Colom is the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche Bruce in 1874 and the first Democrat to win the seat since 1982.
Hyde-Smith had led in opinion polls, and Trump campaigned for her at the close of the race.
Colom's campaign focused on the cost of living, blaming Trump's policies including the Iran war for higher fuel prices.
Democrats flipped seven Senate seats nationally, including Texas, Kansas, Maine, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Alaska is the only Senate race still to be called, with Dan Sullivan challenged by Mary Peltola.

stories.summary: Russia is hiding the true cost of its war in Ukraine, and independent researchers are using gravestones and court records to expose losses far above official figures. Russia 200, a database run by Mediazona and the BBC's Russian service, lists nearly 283,000 named dead soldiers, while the UK Foreign Office and Dutch intelligence estimate more than half a million Russian losses. Russian courts have handed a 14-year sentence to a man who photographed soldiers' graves, and several dozen people have been arrested since the summer on treason charges. Moscow has halted official casualty data, including Rosstat's excess death figures, and restricted court cases declaring soldiers dead, which rose to about 90,000 in 2025. Analysts say the secrecy helps the Kremlin keep recruiting soldiers.

stories.claim: AO3's shutdown after a security incident has sparked fights over fanfic copies on mirror sites and Google Drive libraries.

stories.headline: The Children’s Place Owes Apparel Suppliers Millions
stories.claim: The Children's Place has filed for Chapter 11 and is seeking a buyer, with about $93.9m of trade claims listed.
stories.summary: The Children's Place, the US children's clothing retailer that also owns Gymboree, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 8 November in New Jersey, along with 13 affiliates. The company is liquidating inventory while it looks for a buyer for all or most of its assets. Its 30 largest unsecured creditors are owed about $93.9 million, led by South Korea's Hansae with a $15.4 million claim. The retailer has about $141.2 million of accounts payable and is seeking up to $282 million of financing, including a $166 million revolver. Cascadia Capital contacted about 50 potential buyers, and nine preliminary proposals have been received, though the bankers say none is yet actionable. Stores and websites remain open, but some closures are expected.

Inventory liquidation began on 6 November, alongside a sale process.

The company is seeking a revolving credit facility of up to $166m and a term loan of up to $116m.
Nine preliminary bids were received, but the advisers say none is currently actionable.
Chief executive Muhammad Asif Seemab resigned on 1 November, with John Szczepanski acting as head.

stories.headline: Democrats’ strategy for ending the war in Iran
stories.claim: A Reuters/Ipsos poll finds most Americans want the new Democratic Congress to end the Iran war and reverse Trump's tariffs.
stories.summary: A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday shows Americans want the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on ending the war with Iran, reversing President Trump's tariffs and tackling living costs. Some 71% backed legislation to end the Iran war, including 51% of Republicans, and 62% supported repealing Trump's import tariffs. But the Democrats will have only 54 to 56 Senate seats, short of the 60 needed to overcome a filibuster, and Trump can veto bills. The party itself remains unpopular, with 45% viewing it favourably. The leadership fight and the limits of Congress's power set up a tense 2027 for Washington.

stories.headline: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
stories.claim: Environment Agency data show PFOS and PFOA levels in English rivers fell by nearly a third over the last decade.
stories.summary: Levels of the two most toxic 'forever chemicals' in England's rivers have fallen sharply over the past decade, according to new Environment Agency figures. PFOS concentrations fell by 30 per cent and PFOA by 29 per cent. The decline is credited to restrictions introduced after PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. However, the EA warns that because these chemicals barely break down, their total amount in the environment is likely unchanged, having been diluted and washed out to sea. The agency argues all PFAS, of which thousands remain in use, should be regulated together rather than one by one, a position the chemicals industry opposes.

stories.headline: Study suggests not all obesity means ill-health
stories.claim: Nature study says only a quarter to a third of obese people have clinical obesity, proposing a BMI-plus diagnosis framework.
stories.summary: A new study published in Nature suggests that only about a quarter to a third of people diagnosed with obesity are genuinely in poor health. Analysing almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the researchers estimate that 1% to 3% of people classed as obese by BMI alone would not be, while 5% to 9% more would be diagnosed once body fat is considered. The framework adds waist circumference and body fat to BMI, and checks for organ dysfunction such as heart or liver problems. Senior author Francesco Rubino of King's College London said BMI's inaccuracy is well known but no better system existed. The findings could change how obesity is diagnosed and treated, a WHO-estimated condition affecting over a billion people worldwide.

stories.headline: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
stories.claim: Alan Milburn's welfare review, due Tuesday, is expected to cut some benefits for under-25s and push £bn into youth employment support.
stories.summary: Some young people in Britain could see their benefits cut under a radical overhaul of the welfare system expected from a government-commissioned review by Alan Milburn. The report, due to be published on Tuesday after a year of work, is expected to move under-25s off the health element of universal credit and the personal independence payment (Pip), placing them on the basic universal credit rate instead. Milburn said the plans would not be pain-free and would affect both existing and new claimants, while the exact amounts will not be clear until legislation early next year. The review is aimed at the roughly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training (Neets), and it would also fund more job support. Labour MPs are already uneasy, and savings to the Treasury could take almost a decade to materialise.
key_points: Alan Milburn's year-long review is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the health element of universal credit and Pip.

Under-25s would instead receive the basic universal credit rate, with some eligible for a new additional cost allowance; those with severe disabilities who cannot work would get a higher-rate benefit.
About 430,000 of the four million people claiming Pip in England and Wales are aged 16 to 24.
Milburn proposes billions of pounds for youth employment support, including work placements, job subsidies and personal advisers, with sanctions for those who do not engage.
Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, a rise of 3% year on year, according to ONS data for April to June.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is likely to back the plans, but Labour backbenchers including Bell Ribeiro-Addy have voiced opposition, and savings may take almost a decade.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market impact; mainly a political and fiscal story for the UK government.

stories.headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows
stories.claim: A Capgemini survey finds nearly six in ten large-company executives plan to use more cheaper open-weight AI models to control spiralling costs.
stories.summary: Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to use more cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, as AI bills overshoot their budgets. A Capgemini study of 500 executives at firms with more than $1 billion in annual revenue across 10 countries found that 59% said AI spending over the past year was well above expectations, by 24% on average. Open-weight models handled 72% of traffic on the OpenRouter platform in September but accounted for only 27% of spending, and they were on average 87% cheaper than closed models. Half of respondents would still keep closed models where a task is complex enough to justify the cost. The trend echoes moves by SAP and comments in Anthropic's IPO prospectus about customers shifting to cheaper options.

stories.headline: Trump admin loses fight to spy on random journalists’ LinkedIn DMs
stories.claim: A US appeals court ruled that the DOJ's LinkedIn request for journalists' data was overbroad and must be narrowed.
stories.summary: A US appeals court has sided with LinkedIn in a fight over the Trump administration's attempt to obtain 18 months of communications from journalists. The Justice Department had asked the company for records on journalists who had published more than 1,000 articles, far beyond the reporters tied to a leak investigation into a military report. The three-judge panel, led by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, unanimously rejected LinkedIn's request to quash the order entirely but told the lower court to substantially narrow it. The ruling said the lower court had wrongly treated logistical feasibility as enough to approve the request. It also backed LinkedIn's proposal to notify a single attorney at the outlet under investigation. Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, called it an important ruling for privacy and press freedom.
key_points: The DOJ sought 18 months of LinkedIn communications from journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles.
The request was not limited to reporters linked to the leak investigation into a report about confidential military information abroad.

Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, and press freedom groups including the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press welcomed the ruling.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; a minor reputational point for Microsoft.

The September 2026 flight reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, but a failed engine cut the mission short. NASA says the programme is at least two years behind schedule for Artemis, which now requires Starship to meet an Artemis III deadline in summer 2027. Musk says the next flight will attempt to catch both the rocket and its booster.

stories.headline: A new camera technology could dramatically improve how smartphones take photos at night
stories.claim: Metalenz has acquired PxE Holographic Imaging, whose HoloCoder tech could boost smartphone low-light capture, but it is not yet in any phone.
stories.summary: A Boston company, Metalenz, has bought PxE Holographic Imaging, the developer of HoloCoder, a technology that could make smartphone cameras far better at night. Instead of a standard colour filter that blocks roughly 60% of incoming light, HoloCoder uses a microscopic optical layer to bend different wavelengths toward the correct pixels, and PxE claims sensors can collect up to 2.5 times more light without getting bigger. The same sensor could also capture depth information, potentially removing the need for separate depth-sensing hardware. Metalenz is also eyeing robotics and autonomous vehicles. However, the technology has not yet been shown in a commercial phone, and no manufacturer has confirmed plans to use it. Metalenz expects consumer electronics adoption by late 2027 or early 2028, so this is a longer-term development for phone buyers.

SpaceXSI has taken its own 24 employee apps offline but has not removed the others, and it did not commit to contacting owners. This is at least the third privacy problem for the company involving Grok.

stories.claim: Greenpeace has logged over 500 oil spills since the US-Iran war began, covering about 20,000 sq km, threatening Gulf ecosystems.

Greenpeace has identified more than 500 spills through satellite monitoring, and October was the worst month with more than 30 attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Scientists warn that oil coating mangroves and birds, combined with shallow warm waters, could cause lasting damage to corals, fish and turtle habitats. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's busiest oil shipping routes, so the attacks also bear on global oil supply and prices.

Shorelines and protected areas, including Shidvar Island and the Musandam national park, have been affected.

stories.headline: Quebec’s strategic maple-syrup reserve is running dry
stories.claim: Quebec's strategic maple syrup reserve is nearly empty and expected to be fully depleted by end of February.
stories.summary: Quebec's world-first strategic maple syrup reserve is set to be completely depleted by the end of February, according to the producers' body PPAQ. The reserve, spread across three warehouses and able to hold about 60 million kilograms, was created in 2000 to stabilise prices and supply. Its stock stood at about 18 million kilograms in February, and the PPAQ says strong demand, especially from the United States, has been drawing it down. Quebec produces about 90% of Canada's maple syrup and over 70% of the world's supply. The $1.2 billion industry relies on weather for sap flow, so a bad harvest would leave the market with little buffer. The PPAQ says the reserve needs replenishing and the sector must expand to meet demand. Canadian maple exports are rising, while the reserve's depletion reflects processors buying up stock rather than a shortage at the farm level.
key_points: Quebec's PPAQ says the strategic maple syrup reserve will be completely depleted by the end of February.

stories.headline: UK fraudster who invented ‘too good to be true’ takeover bid given suspended sentence
stories.claim: UK fraudster who faked a £154m takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration gets two-year suspended sentence.
stories.summary: A British man who invented a fake £154 million takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration has been spared jail. Christopher Woolcott, 44, used ChatGPT to create false bank, law firm and private equity documents, and met the chief executive in person while posing as an American buyer's agent. He had bought shares in the Canadian oil and gas company, which is listed in London, and stood to make about £70,000 if the fake deal had leaked. Southwark Crown Court heard that Touchstone's executives quickly spotted the papers as amateurish. Judge Usha Karu handed him a two-year sentence, suspended for two years, plus 200 hours of community service and £4,627 in costs. The case highlights how easily fabricated deal rumours can be spread on social platforms, and it is a reminder of the market-abuse risks around small-cap takeover speculation.
key_points: Christopher Woolcott, 44, pleaded guilty to fraud and three counts of making a false instrument.
He posed as an agent for buyers of Touchstone Exploration, a Canada-based firm listed on the London Stock Exchange, using a fabricated £154m bid.
He used ChatGPT to make fake documents and downloaded corporate logos from Google.
He had bought Touchstone shares and could have made roughly £70,000 if the fake deal had leaked.
Sentenced at Southwark Crown Court to two years, suspended for two years, with 200 hours of community service and £4,627 costs.
He also promoted the supposed deal on Discord to push up the share price.

stories.headline: After historic losses, California GOP faces a fight over its future
stories.claim: California's Republican Party chair Corrin Rankin will not seek re-election, after heavy losses in the midterms.
stories.summary: California Republican Party chair Corrin Rankin said she will not seek re-election next year, after the party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. The GOP is projected to lose at least half of its eight seats in the 52-member congressional delegation and could fall to its fewest state legislative seats since 1875-76. Democrats outnumber Republicans by 20 points in voter registration, and the state GOP raised about $3.3 million this year against nearly $40.9 million for the Democrats. Rankin's exit opens a contest in which state senator Tony Strickland, congressmen James Gallagher and gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton are mentioned as possible successors, though all three lost their own races. Critics, including Assemblyman Carl DeMaio, say the party needs a fundamental restructuring, not just a new chair.

stories.headline: NASA’s secret weapon in the lunar space race may be … procurement reform?
stories.claim: NASA has awarded and opened a rapid run of lunar contracts under a flexible, DARPA-style procurement model for its Moon Base programme.
stories.summary: NASA has pushed out a rapid series of lunar contracts in a single week, covering landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power, storage and communications satellites. Ars Technica argues the most important shift is procurement: NASA is using two-step, DARPA-style calls where companies submit short white papers before preparing full proposals. The agency is spreading work across major contractors such as Lockheed Martin, SpaceX and Blue Origin and newer firms such as Impulse Space and Relativity Space. Funding partly comes from the Lunar Gateway programme, which was shut down, with the $2.6 billion Gateway allocation from the 2025 budget law cited. stories.headline: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
stories.claim: The European Commission has proposed a Digital Fairness Act targeting loot boxes, addictive design and influencer marketing.
stories.summary: The European Commission has published a draft Digital Fairness Act that targets online practices seen as exploiting consumers, including loot boxes, addictive design features, misleading prices and undisclosed influencer marketing. The rules could reach platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, Meta, AI chatbots and language apps. The Commission estimates EU consumers could save up to €13.7 billion (about $15.1 billion) a year. Fines for breaches could reach 6% of worldwide annual turnover. As a draft, the proposal must still pass through the European Parliament and the Council, and gaming organisations have criticised the restrictions on virtual currencies and micro-transactions for minors.

stories.headline: AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM

The technology, Mext, was acquired from a company of the same name in June and uses machine learning models running on a single CPU core to move memory pages between DRAM and cheaper NVMe flash before applications need them. AMD says the software could cut enterprise server costs by up to 83 percent and that 145 systems already run it, saving customers about $5 million in DRAM costs. The Register notes that tests show performance falling to 80 percent with only a quarter of memory in DRAM, and that virtualised environments need one core per VM. The software will be exclusive to AMD hardware and sold as a licence through OEM partners, as memory remains tight in AI data centres.

stories.headline: Olive Young Accelerates U.S. Expansion With 5 New California Stores by H1 2027
stories.claim: Olive Young plans five more California stores by the first half of 2027, expanding its US footprint.
stories.summary: South Korean beauty retailer Olive Young is expanding in the United States with five new stores in California, due to open by the first half of 2027. The locations include Irvine Spectrum Center, Del Amo Fashion Center, Bloom on Third, Brea Mall and Fashion Valley in San Diego, with three of the malls operated by Simon Property Group. The company says its US stores aim to showcase K-beauty and help emerging Korean brands reach mainstream US shoppers.
